newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany pushes for strict EMU terms, tackles reform.
newsitem.headline: Germany pushes for strict EMU terms, tackles reform.

text.p: Germany on Monday denied reports that it had abandoned efforts to insist on the very highest standards for entry to Europe's monetary union and also launched a new bid to hurry along domestic structural reform.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel denied press reports that Bonn had relaxed its hard-line stance on entry conditions for European monetary union, sticking by his established rhetoric on the interpretation of the budget criteria.

Responding to reports in the British press which claimed that Waigel -- who has always been a strong proponent of a strict application of the entry test -- had now softened his position, the minister made clear his views were unchanged.

Referring to a requirement that the budget deficits of those nations which wish to join EMU stand at no more than three percent of gross domestic product, Waigel said "three percent is three percent and it will stay that way".
In Basle, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said he had percieved no change in policy at a meeting of finance ministers this weekend in the Dutch seaside resort of Noordwijk.
"When I was in Noordwijk, and I was there, I had not heard of any change," he said.

Germany, dogged by record unemployment, is scrambling to cut its budget deficit to the required level this year, but at the same time is pressing ahead with much-needed structural reform to help improve its economic competitiveness.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who last week gave Germany's EMU efforts a new lease of life with his decision to stand for re-election in 1998, on Monday gave new urgency to plans for a sweeping tax reform by offering new cross-party talks.

Buoyed by the momentum he gained with his announcement last week that he would stand for a record fifth term next year, Kohl ended weeks of shadow-boxing by saying he was ready personally to join a new round of talks with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).
"If the SPD thinks we must discuss the tax reforms in a big group to achieve a result...then I have no objections," Kohl said before a meeting of Christian Democrat (CDU) leaders.
Both sides met earlier this year to seek a compromise deal on Waigel's plans to cut income and corporate tax 30 billion marks over the next two years.
But, after only two meetings, the SPD walked out in protest at separate government plans to cut coal subsidies.

The tax burden faced by German companies, which is one of the highest in the world, has been repeatedly blamed for the creating Germany's lengthy jobless queues, which have in turn exacerbated its deficit position.
Countries wishing to meld their currencies in the euro from 1999 must meet economic targets this year on interest and exchange rates, inflation, deficits and public debt levels.

Unemployment hit record levels of around 4.7 million in the first months of this year and the government has made clear that it must fall if Germany is to succeed in cutting back its budget deficit for the launch of the single currency.
But better labour market news appears to be on the horizon.
Sources who had gained access to data from the Federal Labour Office told Reuters that German unemployment fell in March to 4.48 million, down 190,000 from February's 64-year record of 4.67 million.

The number of people out of work, based on unadjusted data, fell in both the richer western part of Germany and in the formerly communist east, the sources said. The Labour Office is due to release official jobless data on Tuesday.

Yet neither the official rhetoric on the criteria, nor the signs of greater economic strength were able to convince independent analysts that, in the end, politics would not prevail over economics in the choice of EMU entrants.
"The project remains on target and politics is obviously the driving force -- not economics," said Michael O'Hanlon, chief international economist at PaineWebber in London.

John Butler, senior fixed income analyst at WestLB bank in Duesseldorf, said, "The German government has been waiting for the right time to admit to the markets that yes, it looks like a political solution will be found to allow EMU to go ahead on time, with a fairly large group."

Although many Germans are wary of a single currency, which they fear will be les stable than the cherished mark, a survey issued on Monday showed that most did not want the election next year to be fought on this issue.
A leading pollster said Germans seemed happy to let Kohl -- Europe's strongest backer of economic and monetary union (EMU) -- take care of the problem.
But a Social Democratic front-runner to challenge Chancellor Helmut Kohl in Germany's 1998 general election said he believed the planned Euro should be a campaign issue.
Such an important issue "cannot be made into a taboo," Gerhard Schroeder told the Neue Ruhr Zeitung. Otherwise, he said, "fears will mount and they will not be calmed".
